name: Cold compress / chilled washcloth

lead: A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a simple way people try to reduce puffiness around the eyes. The cold is said to narrow vessels and limit fluid.
Cold therapy has been studied for injury and post-surgical swelling, with mixed results, but no trial was found on cosmetic under-eye puffiness.

paras: Cold lowers tissue temperature and causes vasoconstriction; compression limits fluid leaking from vessels. In sustained cold, a cycle of vasoconstriction followed by vasodilation can occur.
Ice applied directly to skin can cause a cold burn, and uncontrolled cooling devices have been linked to frostbite and severe tissue damage. A cloth barrier is described as safer.

lead: A cold compress or chilled washcloth is a home practice of holding a cold, damp cloth, gel pack or similar item against the closed eyes to reduce puffiness, often after waking.

Cold therapy generally is used for pain and swelling after soft-tissue injury and some surgeries, including facial surgery. Cold lowers tissue temperature and constricts vessels, while compression limits fluid leakage.[1] Evidence for cryotherapy is mixed, and one systematic review found insufficient evidence in ankle sprains.[1]
No clinical study of cold compresses for cosmetic periorbital puffiness was found; the evidence above concerns injuries and surgery.

paras: Cold slows metabolism and constricts blood vessels; after roughly ten minutes of intense cold a hunting reaction of alternating vasoconstriction and vasodilation is described.[1] Whether brief eye-area use produces visible changes has not been formally studied.
Direct ice on skin can cause a cryoburn, and wraps with a protective layer are described as safer.[1] Continuous cooling machines have led to reported frostbite and, in severe cases, tissue loss.[1]

No studies found on cold compresses for under-eye puffiness. Related research on cold compression after facial surgery reports reduced pain and swelling, with mixed results across other conditions.[1]
